Sequence Clustering

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland

Kamila Misiejuk

FernUniversität in Hagen, Germany
Source: vignettes/clustering.Rmd
clustering.Rmd

A transition network estimated from all sequences describes an average process, which may describe none of the units that produced it. Clustering divides the sequences into groups whose members resemble each other more than they resemble the members of other groups, and a network can then be estimated for each group (López-Pernas, Tikka & Saqr 2025). Nestimate (Saqr, López-Pernas & Misiejuk 2026) clusters sequences by the dissimilarity between them or with a mixture of Markov models, and turns either clustering into one network per cluster.

Step Function
Cluster by dissimilarity build_clusters()
Compare numbers of clusters, distances and methods cluster_choice()
Check a clustering cluster_diagnostics()
Cluster with a mixture Markov model build_mmm(), cluster_mmm(), compare_mmm()
One network per cluster build_network() on a clustering
Clustering and networks in one call cluster_network()
Compare the clusters’ networks permutation()

Data

human_long holds the coded human turns of 429 human-AI pair-programming (“vibe coding”) sessions, one row per action, coded into three clusters of codes: Directive, Evaluative and Metacognitive. The network holds one sequence per session, ordered by order_in_session; the timestamp column has the resolution of a day and would split the sessions that run over two days. Sessions range from 1 to 164 actions. Vibe coding, programming by conversation with an AI assistant (Sarkar & Drosos 2025), has been studied with transition networks and sequence analysis (Saqr, Misiejuk & López-Pernas 2026; Misiejuk et al. 2026).

library(Nestimate)
#> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'Nestimate':
#>   method            from       
#>   plot.net_mlvar    idiographic
#>   print.net_mlvar   idiographic
#>   summary.net_mlvar idiographic
net <- build_network(human_long, method = "tna", action = "cluster",
                     actor = "session_id", time = "order_in_session")
#> Metadata aggregated per session: ties resolved by first occurrence in 'code' (76 sessions)

Clustering by dissimilarity

build_clusters() computes a distance between every pair of sequences and groups the sequences that are close (Saqr, López-Pernas, Helske, et al. 2024). It takes the network, which stores the sequences, or the sequences themselves. By default it uses the Hamming distance, the number of positions at which two sequences differ (Hamming 1950), and partitions the sequences around medoids (PAM; Kaufman & Rousseeuw 1990), each cluster represented by its most central sequence.

clusters_hamming <- build_clusters(net, k = 3)
clusters_hamming
#> Sequence Clustering [pam]
#>   Sequences: 429  |  Clusters: 3
#>   Dissimilarity: hamming
#>   Quality: silhouette = 0.215
#> 
#>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist  Medoid
#>   1        183 (42.7%)  7.345             111
#>   2        106 (24.7%)  52.766            282
#>   3        140 (32.6%)  14.881            265

The print shows each cluster’s size, mean within-cluster distance and medoid, and the average silhouette width, which compares each sequence’s distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other one: near 1 for well-separated clusters, near 0 for overlapping ones (Rousseeuw 1987). The three clusters hold 183, 106 and 140 sessions, with a silhouette of 0.22.

dissimilarity selects the distance (Studer & Ritschard 2016):

Distance What it compares
hamming the states at each position
lv, osa, dl the edits (insertions, deletions, substitutions, transpositions) that turn one sequence into the other
lcs the longest common subsequence
qgram, cosine, jaccard the patterns of q consecutive states the sequences contain
jw the Jaro-Winkler similarity of the sequences as strings

method selects the clustering: "pam" (default) or a hierarchical clustering, which merges the closest sequences or groups step by step: "ward.D2" (Ward’s criterion, Ward 1963, as implemented by Murtagh & Legendre 2014), "ward.D", "complete", "average", "single", "mcquitty" and "centroid". The Hamming distance can also weight the positions (weighted = TRUE, with lambda setting how fast the weight decays), so that early differences count more.

Distance and sequence length

The Hamming and edit distances count positions or edits, so for sequences of unequal length they are driven by length. sequence_metrics() compares the clusters of a grouped network on any index, here the number of actions (valid_n).

set.seed(2026)
sequence_metrics(build_network(clusters_hamming), indices = "valid_n")
#> Sequence metrics by cluster  [1 indices | 3 groups: Cluster 1, Cluster 2, Cluster 3]
#>   permutation of the one-way F: 1000 iter (BH), within session
#> 
#>  index   group     n   mean  sd    eta_sq F      p        p_adj   
#>  valid_n Cluster 1 183  9.58  3.65 0.61   332.83 0.000999 0.000999
#>  valid_n Cluster 2 106 56.50 29.42 0.61   332.83 0.000999 0.000999
#>  valid_n Cluster 3 140 21.81  4.44 0.61   332.83 0.000999 0.000999

The three Hamming clusters are sessions of about 10, 57 and 22 actions: the clustering separates short, long and medium sessions. The cosine distance compares the profiles of the patterns two sequences contain, normalised by their length, and groups sessions by what they contain.

Choosing the clustering

cluster_choice() fits every combination of k, dissimilarity and method it is given and returns one row per configuration with the average silhouette, the mean within-cluster distance, the cluster sizes and the ratio of the largest to the smallest cluster; <-- best marks the highest silhouette. Its plot() method draws the sweep as lines (type = "lines", silhouette against k), bars ("bars", one per configuration), a heatmap ("heatmap"), the trade-off between silhouette and size ratio ("tradeoff") or panels per method ("facet").

Number of clusters and method 

choice_k <- cluster_choice(net, k = 2:4, method = c("pam", "ward.D2",
                                                    "average"))
choice_k
#> Cluster Choice (sweep: k x method)
#> 
#>  k method  silhouette within_dist sizes      ratio   best    
#>  2 pam     0.497      22.993      [116, 313]   2.698         
#>  3 pam     0.215      21.027      [106, 183]   1.726         
#>  4 pam     0.256      18.870      [24, 183]    7.625         
#>  2 ward.D2 0.775      26.048      [11, 418]   38.000         
#>  3 ward.D2 0.474      20.914      [11, 303]   27.545         
#>  4 ward.D2 0.419      19.445      [11, 303]   27.545         
#>  2 average 0.783      26.365      [9, 420]    46.667 <-- best
#>  3 average 0.776      26.042      [1, 420]   420.000         
#>  4 average 0.770      25.792      [1, 420]   420.000
plot(choice_k, type = "lines")

With the Hamming distance, the highest silhouettes (0.78) belong to average linkage and Ward’s criterion, which put 9 or 11 sessions in one cluster and the rest in the other. A small cluster of very long sessions lies far from everything else and raises the silhouette without describing the data, which the size ratio (up to 420) shows. PAM gives balanced clusters with lower silhouettes.

Distance 

choice_distance <- cluster_choice(net, k = 2,
                                  dissimilarity = c("hamming", "lv", "lcs",
                                                    "qgram", "cosine",
                                                    "jaccard"),
                                  method = "pam")
choice_distance
#> Cluster Choice (sweep: dissimilarity)
#> 
#>  dissimilarity silhouette within_dist sizes      ratio best    
#>  hamming       0.497      22.993      [116, 313] 2.698 <-- best
#>  lv            0.494      17.682      [138, 291] 2.109         
#>  lcs           0.488      20.368      [115, 314] 2.730         
#>  qgram         0.470      20.136      [130, 299] 2.300         
#>  cosine        0.419       0.183      [170, 259] 1.524         
#>  jaccard       0.313       0.359      [162, 267] 1.648
plot(choice_distance, type = "bars", abbrev = TRUE)

With two clusters and PAM, the Hamming, edit and longest-common-subsequence distances have the highest silhouettes (0.49 to 0.50), and their clusters are again separated by length. The cosine distance has a lower silhouette (0.42) and the most balanced clusters (170 and 259 sessions).

Cosine distance 

choice_cosine <- cluster_choice(net, k = 2:4, dissimilarity = "cosine",
                                method = c("pam", "ward.D2"))
choice_cosine
#> Cluster Choice (sweep: k x method)
#> 
#>  k method  silhouette within_dist sizes      ratio  best    
#>  2 pam     0.419      0.183       [170, 259]  1.524 <-- best
#>  3 pam     0.251      0.164       [102, 169]  1.657         
#>  4 pam     0.284      0.148       [4, 169]   42.250         
#>  2 ward.D2 0.397      0.187       [172, 257]  1.494         
#>  3 ward.D2 0.416      0.170       [4, 257]   64.250         
#>  4 ward.D2 0.332      0.151       [4, 190]   47.500
plot(choice_cosine, type = "tradeoff")

The trade-off plot places each configuration by its silhouette and its size ratio; the preferred configurations are high and to the left. Two clusters with PAM have the highest silhouette, 0.42, with clusters of 170 and 259 sessions. Three clusters with Ward’s criterion have a similar silhouette (0.42), but one of their clusters holds four sessions.

clusters <- build_clusters(net, k = 2, dissimilarity = "cosine")
clusters
#> Sequence Clustering [pam]
#>   Sequences: 429  |  Clusters: 2
#>   Dissimilarity: cosine
#>   Quality: silhouette = 0.419
#> 
#>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist  Medoid
#>   1        170 (39.6%)  0.247             171
#>   2        259 (60.4%)  0.140             376

Diagnostics

cluster_diagnostics() reports one row per cluster for any clustering: for a dissimilarity clustering the size, the mean within-cluster distance and the silhouette, for a mixture Markov model the mixing share, the average posterior probability and the classification error.

diagnostics <- cluster_diagnostics(clusters)
diagnostics
#> Cluster Diagnostics (distance) [pam / cosine]
#>   Sequences: 429  |  Clusters: 2
#>   Quality: silhouette = 0.419
#> 
#>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist  Silhouette
#>   1        170 (39.6%)  0.247             0.199
#>   2        259 (60.4%)  0.140             0.564
plot(diagnostics, type = "silhouette")

The second cluster is well separated (silhouette 0.56) and the first less so (0.20); the silhouette plot shows some sessions of the first cluster with negative values, closer to the other cluster than to their own.

plot(clusters, type = "mds")

The multidimensional scaling plot places the sessions in two dimensions so that their distances approximate the cosine distances, with a colour and a shape per cluster. The second cluster is compact; the first spreads widely.

What the clusters contain

sequence_plot() draws the sessions of each cluster and the share of each state at each position; trim = 0.9 keeps the positions that hold 90% of the actions, since few sessions are long.

sequence_plot(clusters, type = "index", ncol = 2, nrow = 1, trim = 0.9)

sequence_plot(clusters, type = "distribution", ncol = 2, nrow = 1,
              trim = 0.9)

sequence_metrics() compares the clusters on the indices that describe them.

set.seed(2026)
sequence_metrics(build_network(clusters),
                 indices = c("valid_n", "transition_rate",
                             "longitudinal_entropy", "dominant_proportion"))
#> Sequence metrics by cluster  [4 indices | 2 groups: Cluster 1, Cluster 2]
#>   permutation of the one-way F: 1000 iter (BH), within session
#> 
#>  index                group     n   mean  sd    diff   g     g_lo  g_hi  eta_sq
#>  valid_n              Cluster 1 170 33.61 30.75 -13.99 -0.61 -0.80 -0.41 0.08  
#>  valid_n              Cluster 2 259 19.62 16.02 -13.99 -0.61 -0.80 -0.41 0.08  
#>  transition_rate      Cluster 1 166  0.57  0.13  -0.12 -0.90 -1.11 -0.70 0.16  
#>  transition_rate      Cluster 2 259  0.44  0.14  -0.12 -0.90 -1.11 -0.70 0.16  
#>  longitudinal_entropy Cluster 1 170  0.85  0.16  -0.15 -0.83 -1.03 -0.63 0.14  
#>  longitudinal_entropy Cluster 2 259  0.70  0.19  -0.15 -0.83 -1.03 -0.63 0.14  
#>  dominant_proportion  Cluster 1 170  0.52  0.10   0.16  1.46  1.25  1.68 0.34  
#>  dominant_proportion  Cluster 2 259  0.68  0.11   0.16  1.46  1.25  1.68 0.34  
#>  F      p        p_adj   
#>   37.95 0.000999 0.000999
#>   37.95 0.000999 0.000999
#>   82.58 0.000999 0.000999
#>   82.58 0.000999 0.000999
#>   70.85 0.000999 0.000999
#>   70.85 0.000999 0.000999
#>  220.61 0.000999 0.000999
#>  220.61 0.000999 0.000999

The first cluster (170 sessions) alternates between directives and evaluations: it changes state more often (transition rate 0.57 against 0.44) and spreads its actions more evenly (entropy 0.85 against 0.70). The second (259 sessions) is dominated by directives, which take 68% of a session against 52% (dominant_proportion). The first cluster’s sessions are also longer (34 against 20 actions, Hedges’ g = -0.61), so the clusters differ in length as well as in content.

Mixture Markov models

A mixture Markov model groups the sequences by their transitions: it fits one Markov chain per cluster and assigns each sequence to the chain that most probably generated it (Helske et al. 2024). compare_mmm() fits the model for several numbers of clusters and compares them with the BIC (Schwarz 1978), the AIC and the ICL (Biernacki, Celeux & Govaert 2000), lower being better, and the average posterior probability of the assigned cluster (AvePP). Each model is estimated from 50 random starts; seed makes them reproducible.

mixture_choice <- compare_mmm(net, k = 2:5, seed = 2026)
mixture_choice
#> MMM Model Comparison
#> 
#>  k log_likelihood AIC      BIC      ICL      AvePP     Entropy   converged
#>  2 -10029.568     20093.14 20162.18 20375.01 0.7957056 0.6128693  TRUE    
#>  3 -10010.545     20073.09 20178.69 20517.41 0.7057432 0.5768109  TRUE    
#>  4  -9997.471     20064.94 20207.09 20658.84 0.6255671 0.6202143  TRUE    
#>  5  -9987.099     20062.20 20240.90 20746.91 0.5868660 0.6028683 FALSE    
#>  best   
#>  <-- BIC
#>         
#>         
#> 
plot(mixture_choice)

The BIC and the ICL are lowest with two clusters, which also have the highest AvePP (0.80). The AIC keeps decreasing with more clusters, and the five-cluster model does not converge.

mixture <- build_mmm(net, k = 2, seed = 2026)
mixture
#> Mixed Markov Model
#>   Sequences: 429  |  Clusters: 2  |  States: 3
#>   ICs: LL = -10029.568  |  BIC = 20162.181  |  AIC = 20093.136  |  ICL = 20375.009
#>   Quality: AvePP = 0.796  |  Entropy = 0.613  |  Class.Err = 20.4%
#> 
#>   Cluster  N            Mix%   AvePP
#>   1        155 (36.1%)  44.5%  0.834
#>   2        274 (63.9%)  55.5%  0.774

In the first cluster (155 sessions) an evaluation is followed by another evaluation with probability 0.47 and a directive by an evaluation with probability 0.30. In the second (274 sessions) directives follow directives (0.65) and metacognitive actions follow metacognitive actions (0.31) more often. The model and the cosine clustering describe a similar division: sessions that alternate between directing and evaluating, and sessions that mostly direct.

mixture_diagnostics <- cluster_diagnostics(mixture)
mixture_diagnostics
#> Cluster Diagnostics (mmm) [k = 2]
#>   Sequences: 429  |  Clusters: 2  |  States: 3
#>   Quality: AvePP = 0.796  |  Entropy = 0.613  |  Class.Err = 20.4%
#>   ICs: LL = -10029.568  |  BIC = 20162.181  |  AIC = 20093.136  |  ICL = 20375.009
#> 
#>   Cluster  N            Mix%   AvePP  Class.Err%
#>   1        155 (36.1%)  44.5%  0.834  16.6%
#>   2        274 (63.9%)  55.5%  0.774  22.6%
plot(mixture_diagnostics, type = "posterior")

The average posterior probability is 0.83 in the first cluster and 0.77 in the second, and 20% of the sessions are expected to be misclassified. The posterior plot shows each cluster’s distribution of the sessions’ posterior probabilities; mass near 1 means clear assignments.

sequence_plot(mixture, type = "index", ncol = 2, nrow = 1, trim = 0.9)

cluster_mmm() fits the same model and returns the same net_mmm object; it is the name under which the mixture model is reached from cluster_network().

Networks per cluster

A clustering becomes one network per cluster in two ways. build_network() on a clustering, from build_clusters() or build_mmm(), estimates a network for each cluster from the clustered sequences and returns a group of networks.

cluster_networks <- build_network(clusters)
cluster_networks
#> Group Networks (2 clusters via pam / cosine)
#> 
#>   Group      Nodes  Edges  Weights         N
#>   Cluster 1  3      9      [0.105, 0.513]  170 (39.6%)
#>   Cluster 2  3      9      [0.137, 0.685]  259 (60.4%)
plot(cluster_networks)

cluster_network() does the clustering and the networks in one call: cluster_by takes the clustering method ("pam", a hierarchical method, or "mmm" for the mixture model) and dissimilarity the distance.

one_call <- cluster_network(net, k = 2, cluster_by = "pam",
                            dissimilarity = "cosine")
one_call
#> Group Networks (2 clusters via pam / cosine)
#> 
#>   Group      Nodes  Edges  Weights         N
#>   Cluster 1  3      9      [0.105, 0.513]  170 (39.6%)
#>   Cluster 2  3      9      [0.137, 0.685]  259 (60.4%)
cluster_diagnostics(one_call)
#> Cluster Diagnostics (distance) [pam / cosine]
#>   Sequences: 429  |  Clusters: 2
#>   Quality: silhouette = 0.419
#> 
#>   Cluster  N            Mean within-dist  Silhouette
#>   1        170 (39.6%)  0.247             0.199
#>   2        259 (60.4%)  0.140             0.564

With the same settings, the two routes give the same clusters and the same networks, and cluster_diagnostics() reads either. The two-step route keeps the clustering as its own object, to plot its silhouettes or its MDS projection and to describe the clusters before any network is estimated; the one-call route goes straight to the networks. cluster_network() builds the per-cluster networks afresh with the network’s method; inherit = TRUE also gives them the source network’s threshold, scaling and estimator settings. For the mixture model, cluster_network(net, k = 2, cluster_by = "mmm", seed = 2026) and build_network(mixture) return the fitted chains as networks.

build_network(mixture)
#> Group Networks (2 clusters from MMM)
#> 
#>   Group      Nodes  Edges  Weights         N
#>   Cluster 1  3      9      [0.092, 0.563]  155 (36.1%)
#>   Cluster 2  3      9      [0.151, 0.649]  274 (63.9%)

Comparing the clusters

permutation() compares the transition probabilities of the clusters edge by edge, by shuffling the cluster labels of the sessions.

set.seed(2026)
permutation(cluster_networks, iter = 1000)
#> Grouped Permutation Test
#> Groups: Cluster 1 vs Cluster 2 
#> 
#> -- Cluster 1 vs Cluster 2 --
#> Permutation Test: Transition Network (relative probabilities) [directed]
#>   Iterations: 1000  |  Alpha: 0.05
#>   Nodes: 3  |  Edges tested: 9  |  Significant: 8
#>   Global test (networks differ overall?): M = 1.057 (p = 0.000999)  |  S = 0.194 (p = 0.000999)

The clusters were formed to differ, so differences between their networks are expected by construction; the test shows which transitions the clusters differ in, not whether such groups exist in the population.
